title: The shell grows in size without changing its shape

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The shell grows in size without changing its shape

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: r(\theta + \phi) = e^{\phi\cot\alpha}\,r(\theta): rotation by \phi equals scaling, so shape is invariant under terminal growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The shell, like the creature within it, grows in size _but does not change its shape_; and the existence of this constant relativity of growth, or constant similarity of form, is of the essence, and may be made the basis of a definition, of the logarithmic spiral.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Continued similarity of the shell”. Scope: molluscan shells, horns and other structures growing by terminal accretion

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: r(\theta + \phi) = e^{\phi\cot\alpha}\,r(\theta): rotation by \phi equals scaling, so shape is invariant under terminal growth

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-05: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Self-similarity and accretion geometry are direct measurements from abundant scans. Both biological constancy and the logarithmic model can be compared quantitatively against alternatives with standard methods.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Segment successive growth stages preserved by whorls or growth lines, rescale them and quantify shape similarity, terminal accretion and logarithmic-spiral fit. Systematic ontogenetic parameter change or a nonlogarithmic self-similar curve would refute the stated biological or uniqueness component.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The mathematical uniqueness statement depends on the precise definition of spiral and similarity.

Shell ornament and damage affect registration.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Isometry of successive increments is a standard outline comparison, and shells with visible whorls are abundant in open image and scan collections. The claim is general for spiral shells and similar terminal growth, and the public sample is broad enough that widespread allometry would refute it while widespread isometry would support it. The analysis is routine geometric morphometrics.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare shape of successive whorls or growth stages of spiral shells, horns and other terminally accreted structures, scaling them to the same size. Persistent shape supports growth without change of form; systematic ontogenetic allometry refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Aperture damage and sculpture can masquerade as shape change.

Some groups are photographed mostly as adults, so early whorls are less often measurable.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If a coiled shell grows by terminal accretion without changing its shape, then within a species the dimensionless conch proportions (whorl width / diameter, whorl height / diameter, umbilical width / diameter) and the whorl expansion rate are constant across ontogeny, i.e. each linear conch dimension scales isometrically (log-log exponent 1) with conch diameter through the measured growth stages.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: For each of 179 ammonoid species, ww = CWI x dm, uw = UWI x dm and ah = dm(1 - WER^-1/2) were computed at every half whorl with data, and the OLS slope of log(dimension) on log(dm) was fitted across all stages (median 16 stages per species, dm from ~0.5 to ~30 mm). Isometry predicts slope 1. The across-species median and the fraction of species with all three slopes in [0.9, 1.1] were compared with the pre-registered thresholds, and repeated using only stages with dm >= 2 mm. For Nautilus pompilius, the same slopes were fitted per specimen and pooled across all 1408 stage observations of the 6 specimens.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For each species with measurements at >= 4 growth stages (diameters), fit ordinary least squares of log(ww), log(wh) and log(uw) on log(dm) across its stages. The claim is supported if (a) the across-species median exponent for each of the three dimensions lies in [0.90, 1.10], and (b) at least two thirds of species have all three exponents in [0.90, 1.10] (shape changes by less than ~25% over a ten-fold size range). The same test on Nautilus pompilius (Thompson's showcase) is reported separately and must also meet (a) for the species-level exponents from individual trajectories.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if the across-species median exponent for any of ww, wh or uw lies outside [0.80, 1.20], or if fewer than half of the species have all three exponents in [0.90, 1.10]. Results between pass and fail thresholds are 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: across-species median log-log exponent of umbilical width on conch diameter (isometry = 1)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'shell' is the externally coiled molluscan shell; he uses Nautilus as the type case and the claim is stated for shells growing by terminal accretion generally (horns included). 'Does not change its shape' is mapped to isometry of conch dimensions with diameter across post-embryonic growth stages, which is exactly the self-similarity that defines the logarithmic spiral (whorl expansion rate and whorl-section proportions constant). Ammonoid conch-parameter trajectories (Korn's ww, wh, uw, dm measured at successive diameters) and Nautilus pompilius 3D ontogenetic morphometry are the public data; all stages present in the data are used, with a sensitivity analysis excluding dm < 2 mm (embryonic / earliest juvenile shell) reported in measured.extra. Species-level values (not every specimen) are the unit of analysis. The dataset file listings on Dryad were viewed to plan this test; no measurement values were downloaded or inspected before this pre-registration. Deviation noted after download: the released ammonoid table carries conch width index (ww/dm), umbilical width index (uw/dm) and whorl expansion rate WER rather than raw ww, wh, uw; ww and uw were reconstructed as index x dm, and the aperture height ah = dm(1 - WER^-1/2), the radial increment over the preceding half whorl, was used in place of the pre-registered whorl height wh (the same test of constant radial growth per turn). Nautilus has no umbilical measurement, so its test uses ww and ah only.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology)

Data from: Intraspecific variation in cephalopod conchs changes during ontogeny: perspectives from three-dimensional morphometry of Nautilus pompilius (Tajika, Morimoto, Wani & Klug 2018, Paleobiology)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Both pre-registered fail conditions fire for ammonoids: the median umbilical-width exponent (0.705) is far below 0.8, and only 8.9% of species are isometric in all three dimensions; 59% of species have uw exponents below 0.8 (whorls become relatively more involute with growth).

Whorl width and aperture height are close to isometric (medians 0.96-0.97; 69-79% of species within [0.9, 1.1]), so the departure from self-similarity is concentrated in the coiling tightness, not in the whorl section.

Nautilus pompilius, Thompson's own exemplar, passes (pooled exponents 0.946 and 1.055; all 6 specimens within [0.9, 1.1]), so the claim holds approximately for the type case even though it fails as a general statement about coiled shells.

Early whorls (ammonitella and first juvenile whorls, dm < 2 mm) are included in the primary test because Thompson states the claim for the shell as a whole; excluding them makes the umbilical allometry stronger (median 0.633), not weaker.

Thompson himself notes a few lines later that the spiral angle 'is not always, nor rigorously, a constant angle' in some ammonites; the data show that such ontogenetic change is the rule rather than the exception in this sample, which is biased toward pachyconic and globular Palaeozoic-Mesozoic ammonoids.

Gastropods and horns, also within the stated scope, were not tested.

Dryad serves downloads behind a proof-of-work interstitial (Anubis); analysis.py completes it automatically. Dryad API downloads without a token returned HTTP 401 at the time of the test.
